title: Breathless after lacrosse in a 20-year-old with asthma
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of Terry Wakefield, a 20-year-old university student who presents to a tertiary ED with breathlessness that started while playing lacrosse. He uses only a reliever, takes no preventer and had a cold last week. The candidate then interprets his observations and his lung function tests from a few months ago, grades the severity of the attack, justifies the diagnosis against the differentials, and outlines ED management, discharge planning and safety netting.
focus: Acute breathlessness in a young man with asthma: eliciting triggers, control and risk of a severe attack, excluding the differentials, grading severity, interpreting spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility, and managing acute severe asthma
diagnosis: Poorly controlled asthma without a preventer
stem: You are the intern in the Emergency Department of a major tertiary hospital. Terry Wakefield, a 20-year-old man, has come in with shortness of breath. He is sitting up on a trolley in an acute bay on a monitor. A nurse is with you and can carry out your instructions. The nurse has taken his observations.
tasks: Take a focused history from Terry and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining. He is breathless, so keep your questions targeted (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you his observations and his lung function test results from a few months ago. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Terry Wakefield, a 20-year-old second-year accounting student. You are not of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin. You are still in your lacrosse kit, sitting upright and leaning forward with your hands on your knees. You are moderately distressed and cannot finish a sentence: say 3 to 5 words, then stop to breathe. You are worried and anxious. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they examine.

What the nurse reports at the start (when the candidate asks, or straight away if they do not): "Terry walked in with a teammate about 15 minutes ago. At triage his resp rate was 26, sats 94% on room air, heart rate 110, the monitor shows sinus tachycardia, BP 128/78, temp 37.2. The repeat just now was resp rate 28, sats 93% on room air, heart rate 114, BP 126/76. He's had about 8 puffs of his own Ventolin since the game, without a spacer. Nothing has been given here yet and there's no cannula in. What would you like?"

How you change with what the candidate does:

  • If they sit you upright and stay calm, you settle a little.
  • If they ask for salbutamol through a spacer (or a nebuliser) in the first few minutes, after a few minutes you can say slightly longer phrases. You still wheeze, your hands shake a little and your heart rate rises to about 118.
  • If they ask for oxygen, the nurse asks: "What saturation are you aiming for?" With oxygen your sats rise to about 95%.
  • If they ask for ipratropium or prednisolone, the nurse gives it; nothing changes within the station time.
  • If they call the senior ED doctor, the nurse says: "They're on their way, keep going."
  • If they give no bronchodilator in the first few minutes, the nurse says: "His sats are 92% now and he's working harder," and you manage only 2 or 3 words at a time.
  • If they ask you to blow into a peak flow meter, you try but cannot give a proper blow. The nurse says: "He can't do a reliable one at the moment."
  • If they ask for an X-ray, blood tests or your old lung function results now, the examiner says these will be given in Part 2.

Opening line: "I can't... get my breath... since the game."

History (give only when asked; short phrases):

The breathlessness

  • Onset: it started while you were playing lacrosse this afternoon, at about 1 pm.
  • Time course: it began a few hours ago and has slowly got worse. It did not come on all of a sudden.
  • Worse with: running, and now any effort, even walking in from the car park.
  • Relief: your Ventolin puffer has helped only a little. You have had a few puffs several times since the game, about 8 puffs in total.
  • Severity: "I can't... finish a sentence." It makes you feel worried and anxious.
  • Impact: you had to stop playing and come off the field.

Other symptoms (only if asked)

  • Chest: tight, "like a band around it". It is not a sharp pain.
  • Wheeze: "I can hear... myself whistling."
  • Cough: a dry cough, with no phlegm.
  • Recent illness: a cold with a runny nose about a week ago. It has mostly settled.
  • Hayfever: you get it every spring and have it now.

Things you do not have (only if asked)

  • Infection: no fever, chills or sweats (apart from sweating during the game). No yellow or green phlegm. Nobody around you is sick.
  • Collapsed lung: no sharp pain when you breathe in. It did not come on suddenly. You have no Marfan syndrome or connective tissue disease, and as far as you know nobody in your family does.
  • Heart rhythm: no palpitations, no dizziness, no fainting or blackouts, no chest pain.
  • Anxiety: you have never had anxiety or panic attacks. No palpitations, no nausea, no clammy sweating, no tingling in your fingers or around your mouth.
  • No hives, no lip or tongue swelling, nothing new eaten and no stings.
  • No leg swelling or calf pain, and no long trips.

Your asthma (only if asked)

  • Diagnosed when you were 12.
  • At 16 you were admitted to hospital with a bad flare and needed steroids through a drip (methylprednisolone). You have never been in intensive care and have never needed a breathing tube.
  • Usual control: you use Ventolin 3 or 4 times a week, mostly around sport, and you wake at night coughing once or twice a week.
  • You had a breathing test a few months ago, arranged by your GP, Dr Jodi Smithson. You never went back to discuss the result.
  • You do not use a spacer. You puff the Ventolin straight into your mouth.
  • Action plan: "I think I got one as a kid... no idea where it is."
  • Preventer: you have never been on one. "I'm fine most of the time."

Past medical history

  • Asthma, as above.
  • Appendix removed at 16, with no complications.

Medications

  • Ventolin (salbutamol) puffer, a few puffs when needed. You try to take it before sport but tend to forget. You forgot today.
  • Zyrtec (cetirizine) in hayfever season. You are taking it now.
  • A multivitamin.
  • No preventer and no other medicines.

Allergies: no medicine allergies. You have seasonal allergies (hayfever).

Family history

  • Mother well.
  • Father has high blood pressure, well controlled on perindopril.
  • Sister Emily, 25, well.
  • Your mother's father has COPD.
  • No asthma, eczema or hayfever in the family that you know of.

Social history

  • Never smoked and never vaped.
  • 1 or 2 beers on the weekend. No recreational drugs.
  • Second-year accounting student.
  • Very physically active, with a healthy diet.
  • You live with your parents. You have strong support from your family, university friends and lacrosse teammates.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you are pretty sure it is your asthma, because you forgot to take your Ventolin before the game. You are worried because you cannot breathe properly. Your big concern is the lacrosse championships in a few days, and you do not want to miss out. You want your breathing fixed so you can get back to playing.

If the candidate asks whether anything else is worrying you, say: "The champs... are in a few days... I can't miss them."

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: sitting upright, leaning forward, speaking in short phrases only. Using his neck muscles to breathe, with mild intercostal recession and a tracheal tug. Alert and talking, not drowsy and not exhausted. Not cyanosed. Sweaty after the game. Height 178 cm, weight 75 kg. No marfanoid features.
  • Vital signs: as the nurse reported.
  • Hands: warm, capillary refill under 2 seconds. Fine tremor. No clubbing.
  • Pulse: 114/min, regular, good volume; the monitor shows sinus tachycardia (about 118/min if salbutamol has been given).
  • Blood pressure: 126/76.
  • Face, nose and throat: pale, swollen nasal lining with clear discharge. Throat normal. No lip or tongue swelling. No rash or hives. No neck lymph nodes.
  • Chest: hyperinflated. Trachea central. Expansion reduced but symmetrical. Resonant to percussion and equal on both sides. Breath sounds present and equal on both sides, with widespread high-pitched polyphonic expiratory wheeze and a prolonged expiratory phase. No crackles, no bronchial breathing. Not a silent chest.
  • Heart: dual heart sounds, no murmurs. JVP not raised.
  • Abdomen: soft, non-tender. Small healed appendicectomy scars.
  • Legs: no swelling, calves soft and non-tender.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Terry's identity and asks whether he is of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin.

Recognises the respiratory distress from his speech and the nurse's observations and acts before finishing the history: keeps him sitting upright, asks for salbutamol by spacer (or nebuliser) straight away, calls the senior ED doctor, then keeps questions short and closed.
check.d: Credit when a bronchodilator is ordered within the first few minutes, together with either senior help or a clear plan to reassess.

Characterises the breathlessness:
check.d: Credit when at least 2 of the 3 are elicited, including the poor response to Ventolin.

Modifiers: worse with any exertion; only minimal relief from his own Ventolin (about 8 puffs in total)
Severity and impact: cannot finish sentences, had to stop playing, feels worried

Identifies the triggers: exercise without his usual pre-exercise Ventolin, a cold with a runny nose a week ago, and current hayfever.
Takes the asthma history and assesses the risk of a severe attack:
check.d: Credit when the previous admission with IV steroids, the ICU/intubation question and his usual control (reliever frequency and night waking) are all covered.

Usual control: reliever use (3 or 4 times a week, mainly around sport) and night waking with cough (once or twice a week)

check.x: Asks about features of the differentials:
check.d: Credit when pneumothorax and at least 2 other differentials are screened.

kids.x: Pneumonia: fever, chills, sweats, productive or purulent cough, sick contacts (all absent)
Pneumothorax: sudden onset, sharp pleuritic chest pain, Marfan syndrome or connective tissue disease (all absent)
Arrhythmia: palpitations, dizziness, fainting, chest pain (all absent)
Anxiety: past anxiety, palpitations, nausea, sweating, tingling (all absent)

check.x: Takes the medication history: Ventolin as needed (tries to use it before sport but forgets), Zyrtec in hayfever season, multivitamin, and establishes that he has no preventer. Asks about allergies: no medicine allergies, seasonal hayfever.
check.d: Critical elements: establishes no preventer and no drug allergies; Zyrtec and multivitamin are not required for credit.

check.x: Asks about inhaler technique and self-management: no spacer, no current written asthma action plan, and the recent breathing test he never followed up.

Asks briefly about past history and family history of atopy or connective tissue disease (appendicectomy at 16; no family history of asthma, eczema or hayfever; maternal grandfather COPD; no connective tissue disease).
Asks about smoking, vaping and other exposures (never smoked or vaped).
Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: thinks it is his asthma because he forgot his Ventolin, feels anxious, and is worried about missing the championships in a few days.
Examination

General inspection for severity: speech (phrases only), accessory muscle use, recession and tracheal tug, posture, cyanosis (none), conscious state and exhaustion (alert, not tiring), with the nurse's observations.
Examines the chest:
check.d: Credit when the trachea, percussion and auscultation are all reported (the pneumothorax screen).

kids.x: Percussion resonant and equal on both sides
Equal air entry with widespread polyphonic expiratory wheeze and a prolonged expiratory phase; not a silent chest; no crackles or bronchial breathing

check.x: Examines the cardiovascular system: pulse rate and a regular rhythm, BP, perfusion and heart sounds (no murmur), and notes the salbutamol tremor.
Looks for infection and allergy: temperature, nose and throat (pale swollen nasal lining), neck nodes, and the skin and lips for urticaria or angioedema (none).
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: RR 26→28 and SpO2 94→93% on room air in the yellow zone and worsening; HR 110→114 white (sinus tachycardia); BP and temperature normal; yellow zone needs senior review and treatment now.

Grades the attack as severe acute asthma (cannot complete sentences, accessory muscle use, SpO2 90 to 94%) and states that there are no life-threatening features (alert, not exhausted or cyanosed, wheeze audible, SpO2 above 90%).
Interprets the lung function tests, giving the overall conclusion first:
check.d: Credit when the obstruction and the significant reversibility are both stated with numbers, plus the conclusion.

kids.x: Checks the patient details and that the test was done a few months ago, when he was well
Obstruction: FEV1/FVC 60% (normal above 74%) and FEV1 3.41 L (75% predicted, below 3.69), with a normal FVC
Significant reversibility: FEV1 rises by 0.99 L (29%) after bronchodilator, meeting the 12% and 200 mL threshold, with FEV1/FVC rising to 75%, back within the normal range
Concludes a reversible obstructive defect consistent with asthma, showing undertreated asthma even when well.

check.x: Gives the diagnosis as severe acute asthma triggered by exercise and a recent viral infection, on a background of poorly controlled asthma treated with a reliever alone. Justifies it with the trigger, the symptoms, his asthma history with a previous severe flare, the wheeze and the reversible obstruction on spirometry.

Names the differentials, each with a feature from this patient: pneumothorax (gradual onset, no sharp pain, trachea central, equal air entry), pneumonia (no fever, dry cough), arrhythmia (regular sinus tachycardia on the monitor, no palpitations) and anxiety (objective wheeze, no anxiety history).
check.d: Credit when at least 3 differentials are named with a reason; anaphylaxis or pulmonary embolism, each with a reason, also count. Also credit COPD as a considered differential: young non-smoker, ratio normalises after bronchodilator, normal TLCO.

check.x: Management

Escalates and supports: involves the senior ED doctor (already present) and refers to the medical registrar, acute bay with continuous SpO2 and cardiac monitoring, sits him upright, reassesses after each dose. Gives oxygen only if SpO2 falls below 92%, titrated to 92 to 96%.
check.d: Critical elements: continuous SpO2 and cardiac monitoring with reassessment after each dose, and oxygen only if SpO2 is below 92%, titrated to 92 to 96%. Positioning and naming the registrar are not required for credit.

check.x: Gives salbutamol at the correct dose for severe asthma: 100 microgram pMDI with a spacer, 12 puffs every 20 minutes for the first hour (or 5 mg nebulised every 20 minutes: oxygen-driven if SpO2 is below 92%, otherwise air-driven).
Adds ipratropium for severe asthma: 21 microgram pMDI with a spacer, 8 puffs every 20 minutes for the first hour (or 500 microgram nebulised every 20 minutes for the first hour).
Gives a systemic corticosteroid within the first hour: prednisolone 37.5 to 50 mg orally (IV hydrocortisone 100 mg 6-hourly if he cannot swallow).

States the plan if he does not improve or develops life-threatening features: continuous nebulised salbutamol, IV magnesium sulfate 10 mmol over 20 minutes, a blood gas, a chest X-ray if pneumothorax is suspected, and ICU review.

Plans the disposition and discharge medicines: admits him if he still needs frequent bronchodilator after the first hour, with a low threshold given his previous admission. On discharge, prescribes prednisolone 37.5 to 50 mg daily to complete 5 to 10 days in total, starts an inhaled corticosteroid-containing preventer (for example budesonide-formoterol twice daily) and keeps salbutamol by spacer as his reliever, not salbutamol alone; if maintenance-and-reliever budesonide-formoterol is chosen, the action plan and first-aid doses must match that regimen.
check.d: Critical elements: starts an inhaled corticosteroid-containing preventer (does not discharge on salbutamol alone) and completes oral prednisolone for 5 to 10 days in total. Credit the admission criterion if given in Q3 or Q4. Naming budesonide-formoterol and the maintenance-and-reliever caveat are not required for credit.

check.x: Explains in plain words why he needs the preventer and must take it, teaches spacer use, and gives a written asthma action plan. Tells him he can play only once he is back to normal and has been reviewed by his GP.
Safety netting

Tells Terry to call 000 if he cannot speak in sentences, his lips turn blue, he becomes drowsy or his reliever is not helping. Tells him to see his GP the same day or come back to ED if he needs his reliever every 3 hours or more often. Teaches asthma first aid (4 separate puffs through a spacer, 4 breaths each, wait 4 minutes, repeat; call 000 if no better and keep giving 4 puffs every 4 minutes).
check.d: Credit when at least 3 of the 000 red flags, the 'reliever every 3 hours or more' threshold and the 4×4×4 first-aid rule are given; the full repeat sequence is not required.

check.x: Arranges GP review within a week and repeat spirometry once stable.

part2.lead: Here are his observations, and a copy of Terry's lung function tests from a few months ago.
part2.patient:
Ask this only after the examiner reads question 4, in short phrases:

  • "Do I really need... a preventer? I'm fine... most of the time."

If the candidate explains honestly and kindly why the preventer matters, you accept the plan. If they simply tell you to take it with no reason, ask "Why?". If they use jargon, ask what it means.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Both sets on room air before any ED treatment. He had used about 8 puffs of his own salbutamol before arrival.
handover.model:
• Read: at triage (15:40), RR 26 and SpO2 94% on room air are in the yellow zone. HR 110 (sinus tachycardia on the monitor), BP 128/78 and temperature 37.2 °C are white. At 15:52, RR 28 and SpO2 93% are still yellow and slightly worse. HR has risen to 114 (white) and BP is maintained at 126/76.
  • Meaning: tachypnoea and mild hypoxaemia with a worsening trend. Together with the inability to finish sentences and accessory muscle use, this is severe acute asthma. There are no life-threatening features: he is alert, SpO2 is above 90% and BP is normal. The sinus tachycardia reflects his work of breathing and the salbutamol. A white-zone heart rate does not mean he is well.
  • Changes: the yellow zone calls for a clinical review, which here means a senior review and treatment now, with reassessment after each dose. Any red-zone value (for example RR 30 or more, SpO2 90% or less, a new drop in conscious state or a falling BP) calls for a rapid response call and immediate senior review. Reassess at once for life-threatening features (drowsiness, exhaustion, cyanosis, poor effort or a silent chest, SpO2 below 90%) and treat as life-threatening asthma if any are present.

handover.model:
• Overall first: a reversible obstructive ventilatory defect, consistent with asthma.
  • Details: Terry Wakefield, 20, male, 178 cm, tested a few months ago while well. Baseline FEV1 3.41 L (75% predicted) is below the normal limit of 3.69. FVC 5.72 L is normal, and FEV1/FVC 60% is below 74%, so there is obstruction. MMEF is reduced at 1.0 L/s. After bronchodilator, FEV1 rises to 4.40 L, an increase of 0.99 L (29%). This is well above the 12% and 200 mL threshold for significant reversibility. FEV1/FVC rises to 75%, back within the normal range. TLCO is normal (93%), so gas transfer is preserved.
  • Meaning: this confirms his asthma diagnosis and matches the history. COPD gives fixed obstruction, and he is a 20-year-old non-smoker with a normal TLCO. The test also shows significant obstruction while he was well and on reliever alone, which means his asthma is undertreated.
  • Changes: this result does not measure the severity of today's attack. Do not do spirometry during a severe attack; treat first. It supports starting an inhaled corticosteroid-containing preventer, with spirometry repeated by his GP once he is stable.

expect:
• Identify: self, ED intern; Terry Wakefield, 20.
  • Situation: severe acute asthma. Speaking in phrases with accessory muscle use. RR 28 and SpO2 93% on room air (yellow zone, worsening), HR 114. No life-threatening features.
  • Background: breathless during lacrosse this afternoon, worse over a few hours, little relief from 8 puffs of his own Ventolin. Cold a week ago, hayfever. Asthma since 12; admitted at 16 needing IV methylprednisolone; never in ICU. Reliever only, no preventer, no spacer. Non-smoker. No drug allergies.
  • Assessment: widespread wheeze, trachea central, equal air entry. Obs: RR and SpO2 yellow and worsening, HR 114 sinus, BP and temp normal; needs senior review and treatment now. Spirometry a few months ago when well: FEV1/FVC 60%, FEV1 75% predicted, FVC normal; FEV1 +0.99 L (29%) after bronchodilator with the ratio back to 75%: reversible obstruction consistent with asthma, undertreated even when well.
  • Recommendation: salbutamol 12 puffs and ipratropium 8 puffs by spacer every 20 min and prednisolone 50 mg orally started (or being given now); please review now, likely admission.

Severe acute asthma, triggered by exercise without his pre-exercise reliever and a viral infection a week ago, on poorly controlled asthma treated with a reliever alone. Supported by: asthma since 12 with a previous severe flare needing IV steroids, atopy (hayfever), chest tightness, wheeze and dry cough, widespread polyphonic wheeze, and reversible obstruction on spirometry.

  • Pneumothorax: against: gradual onset, no sharp pleuritic pain, trachea central, resonant and equal air entry on both sides.
  • Pneumonia: against: no fever, dry cough, no sputum, no sick contacts.
  • Arrhythmia: against: regular sinus tachycardia on the monitor, no palpitations or syncope.
  • Anxiety: for: he is anxious; against: objective wheeze and hypoxaemia, no anxiety history.
  • Anaphylaxis or PE (also credited): against: no urticaria, angioedema or allergen; no pleuritic pain, leg swelling or travel.

1. Escalate: involve the senior ED doctor (already present) and refer to the medical registrar; continuous SpO2 and cardiac monitoring; sit him upright; reassess after each dose.
  2. Oxygen only if SpO2 falls below 92%, titrated to 92 to 96%; drive any nebuliser with oxygen only if he is hypoxaemic (SpO2 below 92%), otherwise use air.
  3. Salbutamol 100 microgram pMDI with a spacer, 12 puffs every 20 min for the first hour (or 5 mg nebulised every 20 min).
  4. Ipratropium 21 microgram pMDI with a spacer, 8 puffs every 20 min for the first hour (or 500 microgram nebulised every 20 minutes for the first hour).
  5. Prednisolone 37.5 to 50 mg orally now; IV hydrocortisone 100 mg 6-hourly if he cannot swallow.
  6. If no response or life-threatening features: continuous nebulised salbutamol, IV magnesium sulfate 10 mmol over 20 min, blood gas, chest X-ray if pneumothorax is suspected, ICU.
  7. Disposition: admit if he still needs frequent bronchodilator, with a low threshold given his previous admission.

• Plain words: the airways have narrowed and become inflamed; the reliever opens them for a short time, and the preventer settles the inflammation.
  • Medicines: finish prednisolone at home (5 to 10 days in total); start ICS preventer daily (for example budesonide-formoterol twice daily) and keep salbutamol by spacer as his reliever; spacer; written action plan. If maintenance-and-reliever budesonide-formoterol is chosen, the action plan and first-aid doses must match that regimen.
  • Red flags: call 000 if he cannot speak in sentences, his lips turn blue, he becomes drowsy or his reliever is not helping. See his GP the same day or come back to ED if he needs his reliever every 3 hours or more often.
  • Asthma first aid: 4 puffs by spacer, 4 breaths each, wait 4 minutes, repeat; 000 if no better.
  • Follow-up: GP within a week, repeat spirometry when stable; back to lacrosse once symptom-free and reviewed.

ddx.dx: Acute severe asthma triggered by exercise and a recent viral infection, on poorly controlled asthma
ddx.for: Asthma since 12 with a previous severe flare needing IV steroids, reliever only, breathlessness with chest tightness, wheeze and dry cough during sport after a cold, widespread polyphonic wheeze, and reversible obstruction on spirometry.
A young man with breathlessness that started during strenuous exercise; asthma also raises the risk.
ddx.against: Gradual onset with no sharp pleuritic pain, no connective tissue disease, a central trachea, and equal resonance and air entry on both sides.

ddx.dx: Community-acquired pneumonia or viral lower respiratory tract infection
ddx.for: A cold with a runny nose a week ago, with cough and breathlessness.
ddx.against: No fever, chills or sweats, a dry cough without purulent sputum, no sick contacts, and no crackles or bronchial breathing.
No palpitations, dizziness, syncope or chest pain, and the monitor shows a regular sinus tachycardia explained by his work of breathing and salbutamol.
No history of anxiety and no tingling, nausea or palpitations, with objective wheeze, accessory muscle use and hypoxaemia.

ddx.for: He is atopic and has wheeze.
ddx.against: No urticaria, angioedema, new food or sting, and a gradual onset during exercise.

guide:
In Part 1, Terry speaks only in short phrases, and the nurse gives the observations at the start. A good candidate asks for a bronchodilator and senior help within the first few minutes, before finishing the history; that earns item 3. Give examination findings only when the candidate says what they examine. If the candidate asks for a peak flow, the nurse says he cannot give a reliable blow. If they ask for an X-ray, blood tests or the old lung function results in Part 1, say these will be given in Part 2. In Part 2, hand over both results, then ask the four questions in order. Terry asks his one question after question 4 is read.

A high-performing candidate treats while taking the history. They characterise the breathlessness and its triggers and quickly establish the risk of a severe attack: the previous admission with IV steroids, no ICU stay, a reliever with no preventer, and no spacer. They screen pneumonia, pneumothorax, arrhythmia and anxiety, and examine the trachea, percussion and air entry. In Part 2 they grade the attack as severe but not life-threatening. They read the spirometry overall first and then by component, with the obstruction and the reversibility in numbers. They give correctly dosed salbutamol, ipratropium and prednisolone, start a preventer before discharge, and safety-net in plain words.

A borderline candidate takes a long, generic history before any treatment and misses the previous admission or the lack of a preventer. They may call the spirometry "abnormal" without naming obstruction and reversibility, or confuse it with COPD. They may give doses without a spacer or no steroid. Sending him home on salbutamol alone, or waiting to finish the history before treating a patient who cannot complete sentences, is a serious safety concern.
explain:
Diagnosis: acute severe asthma on poorly controlled asthma

Terry has an acute exacerbation of asthma. It was triggered by strenuous exercise without his usual pre-exercise reliever and by a viral upper respiratory infection a week ago, during hayfever season. The diagnosis rests on:

  • the trigger (exercise, a recent cold, atopy)
  • the symptoms: chest tightness, wheeze, dry cough and breathlessness that worsened over a few hours with little relief from salbutamol
  • his history: asthma since 12, with a previous severe flare at 16 that needed admission and IV methylprednisolone
  • widespread polyphonic expiratory wheeze on examination
  • reversible airflow obstruction on spirometry

His background asthma is poorly controlled and undertreated. He uses a reliever alone, has no preventer, uses no spacer, has no current written action plan, and had significant obstruction even when well.

The history: what makes an attack dangerous

Ask every patient with acute asthma about markers of risk for a severe or fatal attack:

  • previous ICU admission or intubation
  • hospital admission or ED visits in the past
  • a need for systemic steroids
  • heavy or increasing reliever use
  • no inhaled corticosteroid
  • poor adherence or poor technique
  • no written action plan

Terry has several of these. Also ask about the triggers: exercise, viral infection, allergens, smoke and cold air. Ask about home treatment already given, and how many puffs.

Differentials to rule out

  • Pneumonia: fever, chills, sweats, a productive or purulent cough, sick contacts.
  • Pneumothorax: sudden breathlessness, sharp pleuritic chest pain, Marfan syndrome or another connective tissue disorder, tachycardia. Asthma itself raises the risk, so always check the trachea, percussion and air entry.
  • Arrhythmia: palpitations, dizziness or loss of consciousness, chest pain. Terry's monitor shows a regular sinus tachycardia that fits his work of breathing and the salbutamol.
  • Anxiety: a history of anxiety, palpitations, nausea, sweating. This is a diagnosis of exclusion in a patient with objective wheeze and hypoxaemia.
  • Anaphylaxis: wheeze with urticaria, lip or tongue swelling, or exposure to a new food or a sting. Terry has none of these, and his breathlessness built up gradually during exercise.
  • Pulmonary embolism: can cause tachycardia and hypoxaemia, but Terry has no pleuritic pain, leg swelling, immobility or long travel, and widespread wheeze points to the airways.

Grading severity (Australian Asthma Handbook)

  • Mild to moderate: can walk and speak in whole sentences.
  • Severe: any of: cannot complete sentences in one breath, uses accessory muscles or has a tracheal tug or recession, obvious respiratory distress, SpO2 90 to 94%.
  • Life-threatening: any of: drowsiness, collapse or exhaustion, cyanosis, poor respiratory effort or a silent chest, SpO2 below 90%, unable to speak.

Terry has severe acute asthma without life-threatening features. Do not delay treatment for a peak flow or spirometry in a severe attack.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: RR and SpO2 are in the yellow zone and worsening, which calls for a clinical review, here a senior review with treatment now. Sinus tachycardia is expected from his work of breathing and the salbutamol. Any red-zone value calls for a rapid response.
  • Lung function tests: give the overall assessment first, then the components. An FEV1/FVC below the lower limit of normal (here 74%) means obstruction; the FEV1 (here 75% predicted) indicates its severity. Asthma is reversible: FEV1 rises by at least 12% and at least 200 mL after bronchodilator. Terry's FEV1 rose by 0.99 L (29%), and the ratio rose from 60% to 75%, back within the normal range. COPD is a fixed obstructive defect, often with a reduced TLCO in emphysema. Terry's TLCO is normal, and he is a young non-smoker. These tests were done when he was well. They confirm the diagnosis and show undertreated disease, but they do not measure today's attack.

Management of severe acute asthma in adults (Australian Asthma Handbook, eTG)

  1. Escalate and monitor: senior help, continuous SpO2 and cardiac monitoring, sit upright, reassess frequently.
  2. Oxygen: only for hypoxaemia, titrated to SpO2 92 to 96% (TSANZ). Drive any nebuliser with oxygen only if he is hypoxaemic (SpO2 below 92%); otherwise use air.
  3. Salbutamol: 100 microgram pMDI with a spacer, 12 puffs every 20 minutes for the first hour (3 doses), or sooner if needed. Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg is an alternative. Use continuous nebulisation if the attack is life-threatening.
  4. Ipratropium: added for severe and life-threatening asthma. Give 21 microgram pMDI with a spacer, 8 puffs every 20 minutes for the first hour, or 500 microgram nebulised every 20 minutes for the first hour.
  5. Systemic corticosteroid within the first hour: prednisolone 37.5 to 50 mg orally, continued daily for 5 to 10 days. If he cannot take oral medicine, give IV hydrocortisone 100 mg 6-hourly.
  6. Poor response or life-threatening features: IV magnesium sulfate 10 mmol over 20 minutes, a blood gas (a normal or rising pCO2 in a breathless asthmatic is ominous), and ICU involvement. A chest X-ray is not routine; get one if a pneumothorax or another complication is suspected, or if he is not responding.
  7. Disposition: admit if he still needs frequent bronchodilator or has ongoing hypoxaemia. Keep a low threshold given his previous severe flare.

Discharge and GP review

  • Preventer: start an inhaled corticosteroid-containing preventer (for example budesonide-formoterol twice daily) and keep salbutamol by spacer as his reliever; if maintenance-and-reliever budesonide-formoterol is chosen, the action plan and first-aid doses must match that regimen. The Australian Asthma Handbook does not recommend salbutamol (SABA)-only treatment for adults; after a severe attack he needs regular ICS-containing treatment. Complete the prednisolone course at home (5 to 10 days in total).
  • Adherence and technique: check adherence and inhaler technique, and use the MDI with a spacer.
  • Written asthma action plan: give him one and go through it.
  • Exercise: a reliever and a warm-up before sport.
  • Resources: National Asthma Council Australia resources and videos on inhaler technique.
  • Follow-up: GP review within a week. Repeat spirometry once he is stable, and refer to a respiratory physician if control remains poor.

Safety netting

Terry should call 000 if he cannot speak in sentences, his lips turn blue, he becomes drowsy or his reliever is not helping. He should see his GP the same day or come back to ED if he needs his reliever every 3 hours or more often. Teach asthma first aid: 4 separate puffs of reliever through a spacer, with 4 breaths after each puff; wait 4 minutes and repeat if needed; if there is still no improvement, call 000 and keep giving 4 puffs every 4 minutes until help arrives. About the championships, be honest: he should play only once he is back to normal and has been reviewed by his GP, with his reliever before the game.

On the observation chart, a yellow zone value needs a clinical review and a red zone value needs a rapid response call.
points: Treat while you take the history: a patient who cannot complete sentences needs a bronchodilator and senior help within minutes.

Grade acute asthma at the bedside. Being unable to finish sentences, accessory muscle use or SpO2 90 to 94% means severe. Drowsiness, cyanosis, a silent chest, exhaustion or SpO2 below 90% means life-threatening.
Ask about risk markers for a fatal attack: previous ICU or hospital admission, systemic steroids, reliever-only treatment, no preventer, poor technique and no action plan.

Read spirometry overall first, then by component. Obstruction is an FEV1/FVC below the lower limit of normal; FEV1 grades severity. Asthma is reversible (FEV1 up by at least 12% and 200 mL after bronchodilator); COPD is fixed.

Severe acute asthma in adults: salbutamol 12 puffs by spacer every 20 minutes for the first hour, ipratropium 8 puffs every 20 minutes, prednisolone 37.5 to 50 mg orally, oxygen to SpO2 92 to 96%, and IV magnesium 10 mmol if he is not responding.

Never discharge on salbutamol alone. Start an inhaled corticosteroid-containing preventer, check spacer technique, give a written action plan, teach asthma first aid, and arrange GP review within a week.
